data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dilemma is a category error: Popper's 'preference' is not an epistemic judgment about the world, but an aesthetic or methodological commitment to 'boldness,' making the question of defensibility irrelevant to truth-tracking.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly linked corroboration to verisimilitude (closeness to truth), this aesthetic reduction contradicts his later writings.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory (e.g., building a bridge) requires a belief in its reliability, an aesthetic preference is insufficient for practical application.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Recasting Corroboration as Aesthetic: Just as a critic prefers a complex symphony over a simple tune not because it is 'truer' but because it offers more opportunities for failure (and thus greater achievement if it succeeds), scientists prefer bold theories for their informational content. The preference is defensible as a commitment to high-content inquiry, not as a strategy for finding true descriptions of reality. The 'cost' is abandoning the idea that science progressively approaches truth (verisimilitude) in any meaningful sense, reducing it to an endless generation of complex falsehoods.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
